source_text: Postquam ergo hoc tali gravitate reprehendit, pergit ad reliqua, ac patronum suum commonet, ut his quae sequuntur attendat. Deus igitur - inquit - maris creator et feminae, convenientia generationibus membra formavit. Sed hoc tantum de capite dictorum meorum inserens, praetermissis plurimis omnino versibus, quibus novitas potissimum inculcatur animarum nihil aut carni aut semini debentium, subdit illum meum: Ita gigni corpora de corporibus ordinavit; quorum tamen efficientiae potentia operationis intervenit, omne quod est, ea administrans virtute, qua condidit. Si igitur non nisi per sexum fetus, non nisi per corpus sexus, non nisi per Deum corpus; quis ambigat fecunditatem Deo iure reputari? [n8] Postquam haec itaque de meo posuit, commendat quoniam catholice ea dicta etiam ipse fateatur. Quis non ergo putaret hominem fuisse mutatum? Verum non fit immemor sui; sed similem conditionem arbitratur pravi dogmatis et pudoris, ut etiam illud perspicuo reparetur exitio, sicut hic assiduo durescit attritu. Probat ergo sententiam meam, et ferrum praeiudicii in fidem suam spontaneo defigit amplexu; sed post haec quasi integer virium, autumat superesse quo dimicet. Sic enim sequitur: Post haec quae veraciter et catholice dicta sunt, immo in divinis Libris veraciter scripta, non autem ab isto catholice dicta sunt, quia non intentione catholici pectoris dicta sunt; iam propter quod ea dixit, Pelagiana et Caelestiana haeresis incipit introduci. Namque attende quid sequitur. Hic denuo nostra dicta subiungit: Quid ergo suum diabolus cognoscit in sexibus, per quod fructum eorum iure possideat? Diversitatem? Sed haec in corporibus est, quae Deus fecit. Commixtionem? Sed non minus benedictionis quam institutionis privilegio vindicatur. Vox enim Dei est: " Relinquet homo patrem et matrem, et adhaerebit uxori, et erunt duo in carne una " [n9] ; vox Dei est: "Crescite et multiplicamini, et replete terram " [n10] . An forte ipsam fecunditatem? Sed ipsa est instituti causa coniugii [n11] . Ad quod respondit, quia nec diversitatem sexuum, nec commixtionem, nec fecunditatem diabolus cognoscat in sexibus, per quod fructum eorum iure possideat; sed his omnibus absolutis invenit quod diabolo deputaret, nostramque honestatem nomine timoris incessit, qui inter tot corporum sexuumque munera, veriti simus carnis concupiscentiam nominare. Sic ergo adversum me patrono suo loquitur: Sed iste in his omnibus noluit nominare concupiscentiam carnis, quae non est a Patre, sed ex mundo est [n12] ; cuius mundi princeps dictus est diabolus; qui eam in Domino non invenit, quia Dominus homo non per ipsam ad homines venit. Unde dicit etiam ipse: " Ecce venit princeps mundi huius, et in me nihil inveniet " [n13] ; nihil utique peccati, nec quod a nascente trahitur, nec quod a vivente additur. Hanc iste noluit nominare in his omnibus, quae commemoravit, naturalibus bonis, de qua etiam nuptiae confunduntur, quae de his omnibus gloriantur. Nam quare illud opus coniugatorum subtrahitur et absconditur etiam oculis filiorum, nisi quia non possunt esse in laudanda commixtione sine pudenda libidine? De hac erubuerunt etiam qui primi pudenda texerunt [n14] ; quae prius pudenda non fuerunt, sed tamquam Dei opera praedicanda atque glorianda [n15] . Egi quidem, beatissime pater Flore, in primi operis quattuor libellis causam nuptiarum, causam commixtionis, causam corporum, causam sexuum, causam operis Dei, causam postremo aestimationis Dei, quae necessario, ut operum suorum probitate laudatur, ita eorum sauciatur infamia; ac per totum scriptorum opus, nec formationi corporis aliquid diabolum addidisse nec sensui, inobumbrabilis omnino veritas approbavit; et ideo opinionem traducis de Manichaei luto haustam esse, perdoctum est.
pass_a_gloss: After therefore he rebukes this with such gravity, he proceeds to the rest, and he warns his patron to attend to those things which follow. God therefore — he says — creator of male and of female, formed members suited to generations. But inserting only this from the head of my sayings, a great many verses having been omitted altogether, in which especially the newness of souls owing nothing either to flesh or to seed is impressed, he subjoins that saying of mine: Thus he ordained that bodies be begotten from bodies; yet the power of operation intervenes in their producing, administering everything that is by that virtue with which he founded it. If therefore the offspring is not except through sex, sex not except through a body, a body not except through God, who would doubt that fertility is rightly credited to God? After therefore he set these things from mine, he commends them because he himself also confesses them to have been said catholically. Who therefore would not think the man had been changed? But he does not become forgetful of himself; but he judges the condition of a crooked dogma and of shame to be similar, so that even that may be repaired from evident destruction, just as this grows hard by constant rubbing. He therefore approves my sentence, and by a spontaneous embrace he plants the iron of a prior judgment into his own faith; but after these things, as if whole in strength, he asserts that there remains something with which to fight. For thus he follows: After these things which have been said truly and catholically — or rather which have been truly written in the divine Books, but have not been said catholically by this man, because they were not said with the intention of a catholic breast — now, on account of that for which he said them, the Pelagian and Caelestian heresy begins to be introduced. For attend to what follows. Here again he subjoins our sayings: What therefore does the devil recognize as his own in the sexes, through which he may rightly possess their fruit? Difference? But this is in the bodies which God made. Mingling? But it is claimed by the privilege of blessing no less than of institution. For it is the voice of God: 'A human being will leave father and mother, and will cling to his wife, and they will be two in one flesh'; it is the voice of God: 'Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.' Or perhaps fertility itself? But that itself is the cause of the institution of marriage. To which he replied that neither the difference of the sexes, nor the mingling, nor the fertility does the devil recognize in the sexes, through which he may rightly possess their fruit; but all these having been acquitted he found something to assign to the devil, and he attacked our decency by the name of fear, as if amid so many gifts of bodies and of sexes we had been afraid to name the desire of the flesh. Thus therefore he speaks against me to his patron: But this man in all these things was unwilling to name the desire of the flesh, which is not from the Father but is from the world; of which world the devil has been called prince; who did not find it in the Lord, because the Lord as a human being did not come to humans through it. Whence he himself also says: 'Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me'; nothing, that is, of sin, neither what is drawn from one being born, nor what is added by one living. This man was unwilling to name this among all those natural goods which he mentioned, about which even marriage is put to shame, which glories in all these. For why is that work of the married withdrawn and hidden even from the eyes of children, except because they cannot be in a praiseworthy mingling without shameful lust? About this even those who first covered the shameful parts blushed; which previously were not shameful, but to be proclaimed and gloried in as God's works. I did indeed, most blessed father Florus, in the four little books of the first work plead the case of marriages, the case of mingling, the case of bodies, the case of sexes, the case of God's work, finally the case of God's reputation, which necessarily, as it is praised by the honesty of his works, so is wounded by their infamy; and through the whole work of the writings, truth that cannot be overshadowed at all approved that the devil had added nothing either to the formation of the body or to its sensation; and therefore it has been thoroughly taught that the opinion of the tradux was drawn from Manichaeus's mud.

pass_b_english: After criticizing this with such solemnity, he proceeds to the rest and tells his patron to attend to what follows. “God, then,” he says, “the creator of male and female, formed organs suited to reproduction.” But after inserting only this much from the beginning of my statement, he omits a very large number of lines. These chiefly stress that souls are newly created and owe nothing either to flesh or to seed. He then adds my words: “Thus he ordained that bodies should be generated from bodies. Yet his active power intervenes in their production, governing everything that exists by the same power with which he created it. If, then, offspring come only through sex, sex only through a body, and a body only through God, who could doubt that fertility is rightly attributed to God?” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.12). After quoting this from my work, he commends it, saying that he too acknowledges these statements to be catholic. Who would not then think that the man had changed? But he does not forget himself. He supposes that a perverse doctrine and his sense of shame are in a similar condition: that the doctrine can recover even from its evident destruction, just as his shamelessness grows harder through constant wear. So he approves my statement and, by voluntarily embracing it, drives the blade of an adverse judgment into his own belief. Yet afterward, as though his strength were unimpaired, he imagines that he still has something with which to fight.

He continues as follows: “After these things, which have been said truthfully and catholically—or rather, which are truthfully written in the divine books, but have not been said catholically by this man, because they were not said with the intention of a catholic heart—the Pelagian and Caelestian heresy now begins to be introduced, which is why he said them. For notice what follows.” Here he adds my words again: “What, then, does the devil recognize as his own in the sexes, by which he can rightly possess their offspring? Their difference? But that exists in the bodies God made. Their union? But it is defended by the privilege of God’s blessing no less than by his institution. For it is God’s voice that says, ‘A man will leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh’ (Genesis 2:24). It is God’s voice that says, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ (Genesis 1:28). Or perhaps fertility itself? But that is the very reason marriage was instituted” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.13).

To this he replied that the devil recognizes neither the difference of the sexes, nor their union, nor their fertility as something of his own by which he can rightly possess their offspring. But after acquitting all these things he found something to assign to the devil. He attacked my decency as fear, saying that amid so many functions of bodies and sexes I had been afraid to name the desire of the flesh. This, then, is what he tells his patron against me: “But amid all these things he was unwilling to name the desire of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world (1 John 2:16). The devil is called the ruler of this world. He did not find this desire in the Lord, because the Lord came among human beings as a man without it. Hence the Lord himself says, ‘See, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me’ (John 14:30): nothing, that is, of sin, either inherited at birth or added in the course of life. Among all the natural goods he mentioned, this man was unwilling to name the desire that makes even marriage ashamed, although marriage glories in all those goods. For why is that act of married people withdrawn and hidden even from their children’s eyes, except that their praiseworthy union cannot take place without shameful lust? It was this that made the first people blush when they covered their private parts (Genesis 3:7). Those parts had not previously been shameful, but deserved praise and glory as God’s works” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.4.13).

Most blessed father Florus, in the four books of my first work I pleaded the case for marriage, for sexual union, for bodies, for the sexes, for God’s work, and finally for God’s reputation. Just as his reputation is necessarily praised by the goodness of his works, so it is wounded when they are defamed. Throughout that entire work, truth that cannot be obscured proved that the devil had added nothing either to the body’s formation or to its sensation. Thus it was thoroughly demonstrated that the belief in inherited sin had been drawn from Manichaeus’s mud.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's pudenda libido is the appetite accompanying union, not a created substance of sin.
